subtopic: OBSERVANCE ON FRIDAY, MAY 15

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: OBSERVANCE ON FRIDAY, MAY 15
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw the attention of the house to an event which has particular significance to all of us in Canada at this time. I refer to the observance of Citizenship day, which will take place on Friday, May 15, and which, in some of the larger centres, serves as the climax of what has come to be known as citizenship week.
Since 1950 Citizenship day has provided a special opportunity for all Canadians to consider the advantages that we enjoy as citizens in a great and free democratic country. Perhaps even more important, it serves to remind us of the responsibilities that rest
upon us all as we strive to make Canada even stronger and more united in the years that lie ahead.
Citizenship day has not been regarded as a public holiday or an occasion for festivities. It is rather a day when special ceremonies and exercises may be conducted in our communities and schools; when we can reassess what it means to be Canadian.
As citizens of Canada we can all take pride in our evolution as an independent state; we can take pride in the role we are able to play in international affairs, and in the contributions that we have made and are making toward the maintenance of peace and security in the world.
In 1867 the British North America Act united four provinces into one federation. Confederation was an "act of faith" that grew out of compromise. The founders, English speaking and French speaking, foresaw a great new nation stretching "from sea to sea". This faith in Canada, held a hundred years ago by the fathers of confederation, has now been realized geographically. It remains for us now to realize it in every other way. As we approach Citizenship day all Canadians, whatever their traditions, languages and cultures, will wish to recall the purposes of our forebears, to create a nation broad in outlook, strong in unity and purpose, every one of whose inhabitants will be able to say with justifiable pride "I am a Canadian citizen".

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: OBSERVANCE ON FRIDAY, MAY 15
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the concluding words of the Prime Minister there will be general agreement. I should like to see citizenship week celebrated during the later part of the month of June, so that on July 1 we might actually celebrate our citizenship and all that it means. Certainly Canadians deserve to be made Canada conscious and Canada proud, and to have the pride of Canadians not only in our heritage but also in our destiny. Throughout the years I think it has been said of Canadians that we have been notoriously calm about our country, in lacking that spontaneous attitude of pride and expressed pride in its greatness.
When I was prime minister we endeavoured to bring about one day in the year on which Canadians might join in celebration and on July 1, 1957, and each year since then there has been the celebration on parliament hill. In addition we also provided for the changing

Citizenship Day
of the guard, a course that has brought to Canadians a pride in our country and to our visitors a knowledge of what Canada stands for, which is so necessary.
The Prime Minister said that at confederation the dream was the building of a nation from sea to sea. In my opinion that concept of one Canada is all the more necessary today than ever before.

subtopic: OBSERVANCE ON FRIDAY, MAY 15
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: OBSERVANCE ON FRIDAY, MAY 15
speechtext: As we approach the one hundredth anniversary of our country we must not do anything which will divide Canadians into two classes. Canadians first class and Canadians second class. That is a message I believe Canadians as a whole hold dear, and rather than a message of fear they would like one of faith.

subtopic: OBSERVANCE ON FRIDAY, MAY 15
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of this party would like to associate themselves with both the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition in commending the recognition of Citizenship day and all that this implies in our rich heritage.
We hope that the celebration of citizenship week will help all of us to realize the great privilege we have in living in a country made up of people of different ethnic backgrounds and various cultures, and that we should realize what a great opportunity is ours, to live in a country which supports the ideals of freedom and justice, a land in which we have great opportunities for the flowering of the human spirit. We trust too that the celebration of citizenship week will help us realize we cannot have opportunities without responsibilities, and that this is an excellent time for all of us to think of the responsibility which is ours to build a united Canada.
We live in a shrinking world in which nations are coming closer together. On the old continent of Europe nations which have lived in a state of bitter enmity for centuries are now working out a modus vivendi. Surely if these ancient enemies can live together in a spirit of harmony we here in Canada of the two great founding races can work out our difficulties satisfactorily.
I trust that as a result of citizenship week, and of giving some thought to this problem throughout the year, we in Canada shall be able to learn to live together in a spirit of mutual understanding, mutual forbearance and mutual respect. I trust citizenship week will inspire all Canadians to work to that end.

subtopic: OBSERVANCE ON FRIDAY, MAY 15
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with much pleasure that we in our group join with the Prime Minister and the spokesmen for the other groups in the house to give our support to what has been
[Mr. Diefenbaker 1
said and what is represented in citizenship week, and particularly in Citizenship day on Friday. One of our greatest needs in Canada today is to realize and appreciate just what Canadian citizenship means, not only the privilege it brings to each one of us but the responsibilities it carries as well.
This means being proud to be a Canadian.
I think it would be well to pay tribute at this time to the Rotary clubs of Canada for the tremendous work they are doing in developing citizenship, and in bringing representatives from right across the country to Ottawa for citizenship week, in their program "Adventures in Citizenship". As we meet these young people, many of them from our own constituencies, I think it can be a lesson for each of us as members of parliament. Certainly it is well to remind ourselves that the privilege of being a Canadian carries with it the responsibility of acting like ones as well. As we give this witness in the international aspects of our responsibilities abroad, may it reflect back to us in every aspect of our Canadian way of life.

subtopic: OBSERVANCE ON FRIDAY, MAY 15
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this corner of the house gladly join with the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in drawing attention to Canadian Citizenship day.
The Prime Minister stated that as Canadian citizens we could be proud indeed on many accounts. We are proud of our development as a state, but it is the independence of that state which we would like to celebrate on Citizenship day. However, when we know that we cannot make a single move without the permission of our neighbour to the south, I wonder what we can normally call an independent state.
We have often heard high sounding words on holidays or celebrations of one kind or another.
The Prime Minister also said: We can be proud of the role we can play in international affairs to maintain peace and security in the world. That is true. But, for a small nation I think we have done even more than our share in that respect. When the government tells us that to maintain peace in the Congo- that world peace which we will celebrate on Citizenship day-Canada had to disburse $12,460,000 for the upkeep of its troops in that part of the world, it forgets to add that out of that amount the United Nations owe us $6,369,000 and has no money to repay us.
Since the creation of the UNEF and up to March 31, 1964, in order to help maintain peace and security in the world, Canada has

contributed the staggering amount of $46,005,000. The UN are supposed to pay us back $15,950,000 but it does not have the money to do so.
In my opinion that is a rather substantial contribution to the cause of peace and security in the world on the part of Canada. We have nothing against that. If I mention this, it is only to give an example of the assistance we can give throughout the world for the maintenance of peace. In the light of that example, I feel it would also be necessary to ensure peace and order in Canada so that we can celebrate Canadian Citizenship day.
Whether or not confederation was an act of faith that grew out of compromise, as the Prime Minister stated, the founders, both French speaking and English speaking, envisaged the establishment of a great new nation. Now, I claim that if the other provinces besides Quebec had treated their French speaking minorities the same way we treated our English speaking minority and others, the celebration of Canadian Citizenship day would be better understood throughout the country.
However, that does not stop us from celebrating with the others that great day dedicated to confederation and Canadian citizenship.
I contend that as long as French speaking minorities in the other provinces do not enjoy the treatment given to English speaking Canadians in Quebec, there will be people, not only in Quebec but throughout the country, who will doubt the usefulness of having a Canadian Citizenship day.
In any event we hope that this Citizenship day will be understood better. To be a Canadian does not mean to be a man settled in an ivory tower, impervious to other elements of our Canadian society.
We wish for a more united and a stronger than ever Canada, as the right hon. Prime Minister said. But let us begin by taking action at home that will give us that unity which will enable all ethnical groups in our country to have a share and a place in our Canadian confederation.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: I will ignore the out of order and offensive form in which the right hon. gentleman put his question-

speechtext: I would reply to the right hon. gentleman by telling him that he has his facts wrong. speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ACTION TO KEEP MINES OPERATING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I put a question to the Prime Minister?
Could he tell the house whether a final decision has been taken in respect of Elliot Lake and Bancroft mines, that is will they continue to operate or will the government definitely permit that the plants which produce uranium be closed down because it has decided not to buy or stock uranium in Canada any longer?
Could the house obtain a clear answer in this connection?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ACTION TO KEEP MINES OPERATING
speechtext:
In regard to stockpiling, the decision was made public in the house a week or so ago, I think, by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who indicated that it was not the intention of the government to continue stockpiling. It will be recalled by hon. members that when the decision to stockpile was reached a year ago and announced to the house it was made perfectly clear to the house, to the country and to all the communities affected that this stockpiling would go on for one year only, and that in the course of that year efforts would be made to help the communities against the ending of stockpiling and the closing of certain mines.
Since the decision was reached not to continue stockpiling, in other words to maintain the decision arrived at a year ago, efforts have been made and are being made both to assist the mines, or some mines, to continue; also to assist the communities affected. When there is any concrete announcement to be made on this matter, and I hope it will be before long, I shall be glad to make it to the house.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, May 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Hellyer for the second reading of Bill No. C-90, to amend the National Defence Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before dealing with the matters covered in the white paper I should like to comment very briefly on the question of early retirement of officers and serving soldiers as a result of the intended reorganization. There were some things in the statements of both the minister and the associate minister which I found rather disturbing, and I hope their attitude is not a hard and fixed one.
As reported at pages 3139 and 3067 of Hansard the associate minister and the minister respectively referred to compulsory retirement and selection as though people were going to be forced out of the services against their will. Other countries have had to face this problem, and as the hon. member for Calgary North said last night no person is indispensable or irreplaceable. Therefore it would seem to me that the emphasis in this matter ought to be on election and choice rather than on selection and compulsory discharge.
In that regard I would like to cover one age group which will be particularly affected, namely those people who have had upwards of 20 years of service and are around 40 years of age. We all know it is very difficult for a person over 45 years to become employed, or to seek a new job, particularly because of their difficulties in getting into plants which have established pension plans. I am thinking particularly of warrant officers, N.C.O.'s and privates in their late thirties or early forties, who now want out of the service but are being kept in it involuntarily. Special encouragement should be given to them so they can

get out of the service and get themselves established before they reach an age where they become practically unemployable.
Yesterday the minister was answering my question about the Veterans Land Act. As I understand this act, it provides that a soldier coming within two years of the end of his normal service can make application under it and build his house. It would be a very wise provision if this were extended to cover all the people who will be voluntarily and involuntarily discharged due to the reduction in the armed forces. It would give many people some incentive to get out of service, and would probably lower the cost of the reduction of the services.
I also think-and perhaps this may have been covered by the minister yesterday-that special preferences should be given to the men who are being discharged and who wish to enter the civil service. I commend to the minister and his officials a study of some of the plans that have been used in other countries where this problem has been met. I believe they would find there are improvements which still could be made in what we are proposing to do in reducing the services.
Last year I was a member of the special committee on defence, and I welcome the reconstitution of that committee. However, I hope there is no significance in the very late start that is being made this year. It would be a great disappointment to me if I found that the committee, instead of being a committee of investigation as it was last year, is now to become a committee of justification, as I believe the Suttie committee may become. The white paper on defence was promised to us a long time ago, and at that time I made the forecast that the flowers would be blooming in the spring before we would be dealing with it. My prophecy has been borne out. I played some part in preparing the special defence committee report, and my part was chiefly directed toward making the language more understandable and removing a lot of the redundancies. If someone on the minister's staff had performed the same function with the white paper it would have been a much better white paper. I believe it was too long, confusing and contradictory, and made too much use of cliches which obscure the true meaning. In fact I venture to suggest that those who have been loudest in its praise and loudest in its condemnation have not read the document very carefully, if at all.
Many people are very confused concerning the objectives to which it may lead and, as some writers have suggested, I believe these people are only left with hope because the document itself is pretty much lacking in positive assurances as to what is going to

happen. The first 12 pages or so are substantially a recitation of history. The twelfth page starts dealing with NATO. Of course it is a self evident truth that in a country the size of Canada our defences have to be in alliances with other countries. But in the present state of affairs we wonder whether a very serious look should not be taken at, and a reappraisal made of, our role in NATO, not only in relation to its military aspects but also in relation to its other aspects, because in NATO today we find some very disturbing things.
The focus of NATO activities and worries has moved from Berlin to the Mediterranean, and we have the unhappy situation in Cyprus where two NATO partners are contending with each other with a third, the United Kingdom, intervening between them. We have the dispute between Israel and the Arab states, and while this does not directly affect NATO countries it certainly involves the United States and will involve Britain. We also have the unhappy situation in Yemen which again involves the very structure of NATO.
Having regard to the rapidly shifting positions of the various NATO countries one wonders whether we are maintaining a sufficient independence of movement and freedom of action within our forces. The end of page 12 of the white paper indicates that the government has adopted as Canadian policy the doctrine of graduated or flexible response. This is a very dubious doctrine. It is not accepted by the French. It is accepted with much reservation by some of the other NATO countries. From my experience on the defence committee I understand its chief proponents are some Americans and the Germans.
What is the doctrine of flexible response? To me it means that any attack by conventional, non-nuclear forces would be met by conventional, non-nuclear forces; that an attack by battlefield nuclear weapons would be met by similar battlefield nuclear weapons of slightly greater power, and so on. This doctrine causes doubt in a person's mind, because if you have a bigger weapon surely the attractions of the strength of that weapon are going to be irresistible and you are going to use it. It seems the doctrine is likely to accelerate very quickly into an all-out nuclear war and, to make such a doctrine workable, it means the early release of the control of nuclear weapons to battlefield commanders. If a crisis is hotting up and nuclear weapons are likely to be used, very quickly somebody is going to be authorized to use them, and this authorization would stretch down the chain of command, thus disseminating the control.
National Defence Act
There are various propositions propounded as to how these weapons are to be controlled, theoretically and mechanically, but I am afraid none of them are very convincing. It is frightening to think of a comparatively low ranking military commander having complete control of a nuclear weapon, however small, and in my opinion it only increases the chance of mistake, error or use in panic.
One of the great promises of the Liberal party in the 1963 election campaign was that Canada would immediately enter into negotiations to get away from using nuclear arms. To my mind the last paragraph on page 12 of the white paper obviously abandons this claim, because there it is stated that an adequate force through a wide spectrum is essential to the deterrence of war, and that we have to have the maximum flexibility and the widest possible deployment. If we are going to have the widest possible spectrum of forces, that can only mean that we are going to have nuclear weapons and are going to keep them.
On the following page of the white paper there is reference to the nuclear club, which is defined as being composed of those countries having the means to manufacture nuclear weapons. The nuclear club goes much further than that now, because if the theory of flexible response is accepted in all its aspects it obviously means that the physical control of nuclear weapons is going to be disseminated more widely, and people who do not have the means to manufacture them are going to have control over them in certain circumstances. This is a frightening possibility.
What should be our role in NATO? I hesitate to say because of the rapidly changing circumstances but there are certain things that I think are going to be forced on us. I think the first principle we should be governed by is that the forces we contribute to any alliance should as nearly as possible be self contained and completely self sufficient so that we can maintain in Canada or through the Canadian government the widest possible choice as to their use. Having regard* to the uses to which Canadian forces have been put since the end of world war II and which one can contemplate, I think that as far as possible they should be non-nuclear forces.
Too often, both within and without the forces, there are those who argue the nuclear problem from an emotional attitude. They advocate nuclear weapons because they are perhaps subconsciously affected by the emotional motive. I have seen this in newspaper editorials; our boys should have the best; our boys should not have to fight machine guns with peashooters. These people do not realize that in many circumstances nuclear

National Defence Act
weapons are not the best and in some circumstances can be a positive hindrance in the operation of our forces. The best example of that which comes to mind is the equipping of our brigade in Europe with Honest John nuclear rockets. We have seen demonstrations and have heard discussions concerning these weapons, and it is my opinion that instead of helping our brigade in Europe they limit its utility and effectiveness.
With regard to our forces in NATO, I think the main reasons for stationing any of our troops in Europe on a more or less permanent or semi-permanent basis are political rather than military, and in my opinion the political reasons are three. The first is the effect on the morale of our European allies by the continued stationing of Canadian and United States troops in Europe. As an aside, I also think they have a considerable economic effect in the areas in Europe where they are stationed. They constitute a rather good industry.
The second reason is the necessity of assuring the West Germans that their eastern borders will be kept intact. The third reason, perhaps one that is not much discussed but which may be more important than some of the others, is the stabilizing effect on the domestic political situation within West Germany by the stationing of British, Canadian and United States forces in that country.
So far as the defence of Canada is concerned, the white paper restates some obvious facts; namely, that our over-all defence must inevitably be linked with the United States and that NORAD, of course, is the basis of this link. I think too it is not only the politicians in the heat of election campaigns but also at times other experts who have made statements concerning the kind, size and utility of various weapons which have not been and cannot be borne out subsequently by events.
The main contribution to our defence is the radar system that extends throughout the north. I venture to suggest that the northern approaches to the United States are much better protected by the radar screens and warning system than some of the southern approaches are or might have been. As long as there is some chance of a bomber attack you will get various opinions from people. Those in the field of flying, such as the air force fighter plane pilots, tend to put the chance of a bomber attack rather high while others tend to set it much lower. It is hard to gauge the situation accurately, but as long as that threat continues I think we will have to have weapons of the class of the Bomarc and the Voodoo. It is regrettable for many reasons that the Voodoo squadron should be withdrawn from North Bay. Perhaps the Voodoos are

more useful in the defence of Canada and to world peace than the Starfighters we have in Europe.
There is one statement in the white paper which is absolutely mystifying to me. On page 14 there is reference to anti-I.C.B.M. defence, commonly known as Nike, I believe, and the statement is made that we cannot do anything about passive air defence and fall-out protection until we find out whether we are going to get an anti-I.C.B.M. weapon. It would seem to me that until we do get an effective anti-I.C.B.M. weapon great stress should be put on passive defence and fall-out protection, because if a major war were to break out when we were still not effectively defended by anti-I.C.B.M. weapons it might very well be the task of Canada to try to survive. As we would be on the periphery of the heavy attacks it might be Canada's duty to continue the thread of western civilization. I do not agree with those who say that if war breaks out the outlook will be hopeless and we should throw up our hands. As long as there are two civilized western people alive, provided they are of the appropriate sexes, I think it is our duty to try to survive, to maintain what we have and to rebuild. For that reason I think that as long as we are undefended from I.C.B.M.'s we should put greater emphasis on passive defence and survival. I hope that factor of our national defence is being taken into consideration by the Suttie committee which is now sitting, since our passive defence is largely dependant upon the militia.
The next point is again a recitation of history. The second duty of our defence forces is to occupy our land masses and the sea lane approaches to them. It is a matter of regret to me that we are reducing the physical presence of our troops in northern Canada. I feel the northern bases should be maintained by the military. There was no real saving in this change. I feel that the cost of maintaining these bases under the Department of Transport will be greater than the cost of maintaining them under the Department of National Defence. This was purely a bookkeeping entry to make the Department of National Defence look good, and I think we have lost something of our prestige.
The white paper is largely silent on the matter of patrolling our vast seacoasts and the protection of the sea lanes into Canada. I would have liked to hear something about air-sea co-operation. I would have liked to hear something about whether we would build a simplified cruiser or patrol vessel which would work in conjunction with air cover from our very fine patrol planes.

Since we are on the subject of national defence generally I should like to mention the Bobcat that was scrapped several months ago. I hope when the minister replies he will tell us how the deliveries of the M-113's are coming along; when they are going to be delivered, and how satisfactory they are. When I was last advised on the subject I understood that the Starfighter was completely unarmed and as useless as a Piper Cub for what it was doing. In fact it was more useless, because that plane was being used for training and it is a difficult plane in which to train men. I hope the minister will be able to tell us these planes have been armed and are fully operational. I hope they will not be left sitting useless on the airstrips of Europe for another six or nine months.
While dealing with the Starfighter I should like to bring up the matter of cliches and misleading phrases. This is a very good example of it. The Starfighter, I believe, is described in terms of the trade as a strike-reconnaissance plane. Now, if one looks at the Starfighter one realizes it is a low level offensive bomber. If the Department of National Defence and the people associated with it started calling a spade a spade and giving rather more accurate descriptions, even though they may be unpalatable to people who hear them, it would give us a better understanding of national defence.
The other point upon which we are waiting to hear from the minister relates to what sort of forward transport is going to be provided for our mobile brigade. What sort of forward transport is going to be provided for our brigade in Europe? Are we going to get helicopters? What type of close support plane is going to be provided for an operation such as the one in Cyprus? These are things we need to know.
Of course the white paper is largely silent on the navy. I would not want to disagree with my hon. friend from Calgary North, but there is one type of transport ship we need in small quantities. These could become the joint responsibility of the Department of National Defence and the Department of Transport and could form the nucleus of a deep sea fleet. Britain and the United States are both adopting this scheme. They are building a very fast freighter which has a limited capacity for carrying a certain number of troops. In normal times it can be used as a cargo vessel and have special devices built into it, such as a hard nose for going into difficult places. Its loading and unloading equipment is self sufficient and can be used without modern docks. I think between the Department of Transport and the Department of National Defence there ought to be an investigation of this type of vessel, because it 20220-201
National Defence Act
would make a modest start on a deep sea fleet. It would also provide a training base for sailors on the ocean rather than on the great lakes.
I think I have made my objections to the Suttie committee rather clear. The minister indicated yesterday that it was economics that dictated these cuts in the militia. I hope this committee will not be a committee of justification but is undertaking a real study of the problem.
I come now to a consideration of the bill itself which is the subject matter of this debate and which relates to a reorganization of the cabinet defence committee. I believe we should have a more complete explanation from the minister as to what is going to be the role of the cabinet defence committee. What is going to be the role of the defence council? How is it going to be made up? What authority is it going to have? Yesterday the minister said something that indicated it would only provide an interchange of views. Who are going to be on the defence staffs, and how are they going to be designated? It is true that some of these details cannot be given now, but I am wondering whether we are proceeding in an orderly fashion or if we have started on this reorganization to make a showing without any clear idea of what is going to come next.
I was pleased to hear that there is going to be a program analysis department. This is a completely American idea. Mr. McNamara has it and it is headed by Mr. Enthoven, who is a very distinguished mathematician. In the United States these people are called the "whiz kids", and I am wondering if their Canadian counterparts might be called "Hellyer's hellcats".
Another matter on which I should like to touch briefly is the position of the Associate Minister of National Defence. I have found the associate minister knowledgeable, competent and courteous. I do not want him to think I am trying to get him out of the job. I do not believe I would succeed in any event, because a couple of Sundays ago I was watching television and I saw the minister being interviewed by the Liberal party's favourite part time commentator, Mr. Fisher. At that time the minister indicated that he was about ready to move out of the Department of National Defence and clean up the mess in finance.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is not a fair interpretation.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The position of associate minister has been nebulous and irregular. There is provision for three associate ministers to be appointed for six months at a time, in times of extreme emergency.

National Defence Act
Then, in 1953, there was some change. It was at the time of the Korean war and the government of the day brought in an amendment to the defence act to provide for an associate minister. I believe Mr. Campney had been associate minister under the old regulation and that he was then appointed under the new. Mr. St. Laurent said at that time, as recorded at page 1524 of Hansard, that the need was for an associate minister at a time of emergency, which was something less than a national emergency; he did not say, fortunately, a military emergency. After Mr. Claxton left the department I do not think any associate minister was appointed until the middle of 1957, and I think the emergency which occurred at that time was political rather than military. After the election of 1957 the office again fell into disuse and I do not think there was any appointment until late 1958 or early 1959. All this leads me to the conclusion that the abilities of the associate minister would better be employed in the discharge of another portfolio, and that it would lead to the more orderly disposition of business if we had only one Minister of National Defence.
As I have said, and as other speakers before me have said, I hope the defence committee will be given adequate time in which to study this bill and related defence matters. The steps now being contemplated are likely to have an effect for a long time. They will have wide economic repercussions in this country and their impact on the military structure cannot yet be estimated. I see in the newspapers today that some NATO countries are disturbed about the course which national defence may take, consequent upon this white paper. I hope the delay in setting up this committee does not mean we are expected to be a rubber stamp or that we will not be given sufficient opportunity to discuss the subject of defence in all its aspects.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I will try to be fairly brief in talking about defence matters but I do wish to put a few of my views on the record, since I have not had an opportunity to do so for some time.
I am sure we are all agreed in this house that the only real defence of this country and, in this day and age, of any country, is the maintenance of peace. If we follow that line of thought logically, I think it is apparent that the greatest chance of maintaining peace, the greatest force we now have available for that purpose, is the United Nations. We shall therefore be protecting ourselves in the best possible way if we bend all our efforts toward building up the power and prestige of the United Nations. I suggest this is more than 
just the job of the Department of External Affairs. I believe the peace keeping role of the United Nations could be greatly expanded. The possibility of a permanent force under the control of that body contains the hope that it could some day become the only really powerful force in the world.
I suggest that the role which Canadian defence policy could best fulfil would be to make sure that our forces are so constituted that they could be most readily of use to the United Nations-that they should be so flexible and so unitized that they could be made available to that world body on an ever stronger basis as time goes on. If there were a feeling that we were proceeding along those lines there would be an atmosphere of confidence in the country. We should not take years and years to get to this stage. There is no doubt that any major conflict which might develop at this time could result in the annihilation of everyone on earth or, at least, in the complete destruction of civilization, and it is all too frighteningly possible that this could happen now. For this reason I suggest that our first line of defence is to do as speedily as we can all those things which would help build up the United Nations and bring nearer the possibility of an effective peace keeping force.
I get no feeling of security when I look at what is supposed to be the present defence policy* and even less when I regard those people in whose hands our defence policy now resides. I remember only last year the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), talking about the acquisition of nuclear arms, making it clear in his speeches that he thought this was a real mistake. In fact, on June 7 he made it very clear that in his view taking nuclear arms was a mistake. Yet we have got them. He admitted on June 7 that we could not get them without entering into another agreement, and there was still time to get out of signing another agreement. But hon. gentlemen opposite went ahead and made another agreement to acquire nuclear arms; in other words, they carried out a policy about which they were unhappy-a mistaken policy which they really wished to avoid. Certainly, this is no reason for placing confidence in the government.
I sometimes find a little incredible the lengths to which government spokesmen will go in an effort to persuade the people of Canada that the only reason for pursuing such a stupid defence policy is that they were committed to it. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer), speaking at Christmastime on television, made a statement which, to me, sounded incredible, in an attempt to give some reason why we should have Bomarcs. This was when he said the

principal threat still comes from manned bombers. I thought all responsible people had reached the conclusion at least three or four years ago that the manned bomber was no longer the principal threat. All of us who were in the armed forces during the last war and who were stationed overseas can remember the V-2 rockets. We had never heard of a sputnik, but suddenly V-2 rockets aimed from a considerable distance were reaching their targets with fair accuracy. That was 20 years ago, and it is 18 years since the first atomic bomb was dropped. The combination of the two has been a preoccupation of the military planners ever since and has led to the investment of billions of dollars in scientific research and development in the intervening period.
The position, then, is that 20 years of intensive research have been spent on the development of that original V-2 rocket. Kockets have been built powerful enough to send vehicles into space and circle the moon. We now have sufficiently advanced technology to station satellites out in space and keep them there. The power of modern rockets is almost unlimited. In addition, starting a number of years ago, there have been many demonstrations of their accuracy. As to the possibilities of destruction, we have some knowledge of the size and capability of nuclear explosions. We have learned of the H-bomb, the cobalt bomb and so on which make the bombs of Hiroshima seem like toys. Yet, in the face of all this evidence, in the face of a technical capacity and power of destruction never known before, the minister appears on a national television hook-up and tells us that the manned bomber is still the principal threat. It sounds idiotic and it certainly does not give anyone in this country any confidence that the government knows what it is doing.

speechtext: It is the truth, but you would not believe it.

speechtext:
I may say it is not the first time I have heard the minister of defence make statements which were not particularly accurate. When he was in opposition he was so talkative that I am sure he covered all the ground on both sides to such an extent that today he can turn round and say he has said everything on both sides of all questions. So that he can tell us, whenever he is wrong, that he has also made a statement that is right. I imagine it is a state of mind that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) is in as well. I cannot for the life of me understand why this government still persists in its policy of nuclear arms. I cannot understand why the government has not been taking some fast action to get out of the policy which the 20220-201i
National Defence Act
Prime Minister admits is stupid. This is incredible. I cannot understand why we have aeroplanes sitting over in Europe when I think it is by now obvious to most people that a nuclear role for the 104's is probably unsuitable. It certainly would be much more advantageous for Canada to have those aeroplanes in a dual capacity role, a conventional weapons role, whereby they would be able to take advantage of French airfields and whereby the air force itself would be useful to the United Nations if called upon by the United Nations. I think it would be much more useful if we could make that sort of progress toward building up the kind of United Nations force that we want. I cannot see that the Honest Johns equipped with nuclear weapons are doing us any good. It is obvious from the studies of the defence committee that they are not helpful to that brigade and that they should go to another unit.
I think Canadians have had to take a loss of sovereignty in order to acquire nuclear weapons, and they have not added to our defence but rather have only complicated it. With the threat always being there that a spark could set things off, I cannot emphasize too much the fact that our greatest defence is to accelerate the speed with which we can ready our armed forces, make them flexible and useful to the United Nations; to accelerate our efforts to gain for the United Nations ever greater support and power so that it will become a real peace keeping unit. I think the more we press along this line, the more vigorously are we actually engaging in the defence of Canadians.
I would hope that some time in the not too distant future the Prime Minister will make the announcement in this house that he has finally decided to keep his election promises and get Canada out of the nuclear weapons field; get nuclear weapons off Canadian soil, so we will regain our sovereignty. His statements at the United Nations with regard to a permanent peace keeping force seem to be bending in the right direction and it sounds as though he is interested in it. If this announcement is made, perhaps the people of Canada will then get the feeling that this government is interested in the defence of this country rather than in the political show they can make by dramatic announcements of the money they save. While speaking of the money being saved, Mr. Speaker, I must say I am sure most people in this country are very happy to think we can save something on defence. They would be quite happy to see defence spending cut very drastically, and I think it could be cut very drastically if we had some careful planning and a policy that precluded nuclear arms;

National Defence Act
a policy that envisaged Canada's best role as that of conventional forces available to the United Nations.
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to refer to just a couple of things brought out in the defence committee report of last year, because last June 7 the Prime Minister gave as one of the reasons for our taking nuclear arms the fact that we spent a billion dollars on this equipment. I think this idea has been spread around the country and the Liberals have tried to sell the idea that unless we take nuclear arms, all that money is wasted. I just wanted to point out that the evidence given before the defence committee which studied this subject-and I think the government made available to them the best information there was-does not sustain that argument in any manner. The Bomarc is more useful, they said, with a nuclear warhead, if bombers are the threat; and I say they are not. The Voodoo is more effective with a nuclear warhead, they said, but that is as far as it really goes. Its usefulness has not been demonstrated. The F-104, with some modifications, can have other than a nuclear role. So there is no justification, no honesty, to the argument that all this equipment would be wasted. I think, in fact, that we must consider the complications that arise out of our attempting to get into a nuclear role and our unsuitability for this. We must also consider the fact that many small and neutral nations in the world would have much more confidence in Canada if we were out of the nuclear field and we would be making more friends, and this is always a good line of defence.
I trust that we may in the very near future, Mr. Speaker, have our Prime Minister come into the house and confess that the government has abandoned its nuclear policy, that they are getting out of it, so they will be able to give us some honest statements on defence policy instead of political statements.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the discussion of Bill No. C-90 to amend the National Defence Act gives us an opportunity to express some ideas and discuss some principles which, I think, are directly related to the general philosophy on which our governments have always based their justification, or rather, their attempts at justifying their various defence policies.
Having returned from a week end trip where, with a group of other hon. members, we visited several military establishments, it was very difficult for us not to think of the enormous amounts that have been spent on defence. I honestly wonder whether we

have not started on a wild race toward death and destruction of our civilizations.
In 1961, as well as in 1962, the defence budget in Canada was over $1.5 billion a year. And this is only for two years. If we calculate the interest at 6 per cent, which we had to pay for defence alone, it means $180 million. That is to say, in the last ten years we paid more than $1 billion in interest alone, without considering the large spending for war purposes.
I shall linger a few minutes on this point. We are in favour of passive defence. We also favour a good defence organization. We agree on acquiring all the latest instruments which exist or may yet be conceived.
But we also know that expenses for war purposes are not active capital. They produce no dividend.
We also know that our people must make enormous sacrifices for our defence to be maintained. If the general public has to make such huge sacrifices, I wonder why those who are in control of credit should not make the same sacrifices, which are imposed on the people, because all capital required for defence comes out of the taxpayer's pocket and is borrowed from high finance at interest rates which, I think, vary from 5 to 6 per cent.
Now, it is impossible for a country like Canada, with a population of about 19 million people, to keep up such expenses when these amounts can no longer be found in the taxpayers' pockets nor to be obtained by borrowing at exorbitant interest rates.
War has always existed among men. It was brought about in the course of history under all possible and imaginable excuses: conquest, right, might, honour, for God, for freedom, for civilization. There are, apparently, just and unjust wars.
Finally, in the living world, there is a universal order of which the great rule is the law of preservation of the individual. Up to now, war has only partially violated that rule, maybe not at all since the human species has managed to survive, but when the very existence of the species is jeopardized, when extermination is hanging over the species, war is violating the law of preservation of the universe.
Universe, man and the human species, have the same finality. This basic unit must be preserved and we must avoid a new war which would bring about disruption.
The conflict between capitalism and communism must be overcome and transposed to a superior plane. Inhuman to each other, both civilizations are surely not inhuman to the same degree or in the same way, but it is not

true that one represents good and the other evil. It is not true that we must necessarily choose one against the other. Any propaganda on that basis already means war. It is a mobilization of mind and spirit which leads to plain mobilization.
Capitalism may despise man but the fact remains that, in western countries, man has the freedom to protest against such contempt. No doubt this freedom is relative, but man's conscience can nevertheless make itself heard.
Even if he is penniless, a man can speak, write, express his thoughts and his rebellion, unite with other men, denounce a system and fight against it.
Freedom, up to now, has been powerless, but it may not always be so. In any event, it remains the best weapon in the hands of men.
Despised, man in the western world can voice his complaint. Despised, man in the U.S.S.R. cannot even do that, because his masters have muzzled him. But woe unto the satellite nation that would even attempt to throw off the yoke.
If we are compelled to make a choice between two civilizations, we must choose capitalism, but only as a lesser evil and for only one reason: man in the western world has a little more freedom. We still have freedom of speech, but we are under the yoke of a financial dictatorship which delays progress and prevents economic, scientific, cultural and natural development, since it even prevents human beings from being born and undermines the vital foundations of the economy.
Because of its monstrosities, the one way capitalist system has made a great number of victims. The financial dictatorship spreads more ruins and hate and it has made more victims than the most devastating war.
The conscientious objector who refuses to go to war, not because he does not want to defend his country, but simply because he will not kill, is logical when he does not admit the present system, because that system kills and treats men like animals.
That conscientious objector is infinitely more human than the herds that accept to be led to the slaughter-house. What could the masters of the world do in the face of a general conscientious objection? A first step can and must be made in that direction. Let the nonatomic nations unite to notify the others of their intention to refuse the massacre, and before that tremendous force of three billion men, unarmed but determined, and they shall not dare.
Mankind is more and more conscious of the unity of its destiny. It is not possible it
National Defence Act
should accept to be driven to suicide. Therefore, all men must unite to prevent it. Since we are condemned to live in peace, we must seek as a solution to organize peace. Now,, the only way to organize peace is to replace-material values by moral values, to submit all men and all nations to a basic law of respect for each and everyone.
Any analysis, an analysis of the universe, of man and of the modern world, lead to the same conclusion: to live and to survive, mankind must give onto itself that law as soon as possible. That moral law, which Social Crediters have sworn to defend, is in fact the law of respect for life and conservation of man and mankind.
It is unthinkable that the law of mankind, stated or not, written or not, is a law of destruction of man, of the species. Man will have to accept a law of conservation and respect. It will be neither superstition, nor compulsion, nor slavery; in the last report, it will be the condition of his true liberty, so dear to the human being. The building of the new world will require time, courage and perseverance, but it will be a reality only when all the protectors of society will take their true responsibilities, and will not let the life of our women, men and children be shortened in this way.
And what about the moral results? The hardships imposed on our families by unpayable debts and by the excesses of a financing system and unpayable interests that take away the normal purchasing power of families; abundance calls aloud for vengeance as Abel's blood called out against Cain, and those murders are committed at home, in this Canada of ours, in our provinces, and it does not seem to disturb the sleep of the keepers of society.
On the doors of those offices where killing orders are issued, the commandment that is violated the year round: Thou shall not kill, should be engraved. And on the doors of ministers and members of parliament who legislate for the country: Thou shall not let kill.
So, the murderer is the money system. Those who support and defend it, support and protect a murdering system, those who make it legal, make legal a murdering system, if governments make legal and support the money system which deprives human beings of the necessities of life, those governments are party to a suicidal system.
Financial dictatorship assassinates our men, our women, our children, and puts our governments into slavery. During the war, there were tears and blood, because error took the place of truth. It is the lack of charity which kills people, which leads men, brothers by nature, to fight one another, and not only on the battlefields.

National Defence Act
Thanks to technological progress, we should live in a garden of Eden; God has showered its blessings and gifts on earth and yet how many people do not have enough to live.
When science and finance work hand in hand, what can stop man? How many things can man do when financial obstacles are removed. Financial nonsense is brushed aside for war, but it is restored afterwards, and once again economic chaos prevails.
By way of solution, I would suggest to the government that there is only one thing to do, which is its bounden duty to do; to correct and revive our economy, the credit of the nation should be made available, and then we will be assured of a market for our products.
What we are now doing to create instruments of destruction might tomorrow serve to create a greatness such as the world has never known, provided we have the intelligence and ethics to recognize that there is enough for everybody in this new world.
Mr. Speaker, before ending my remarks, may I say that we are not opposed to the bill amending the National Defence Act, nor to the opportunity of voicing some ideas and discussing certain principles which, to my mind, are directly connected with the general philosophy on which our governments always based their justification, or, rather their attempts at justifying their various defence policies in the house.
Moreover, though we do not always tacitly accept the priority given to defence problems, we are ready to face those problems and to discuss them, so that possible decisions might better express the feeling of the Canadian people which we all represent here, in this house.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, I cannot but voice some anxiety with regard to the results of this bill, if it is passed. For my part, I met several veterans who expressed worries similar to mine in this respect.
Each one of us here recognizes the greatness, the value of the Canadian forces. Indeed, our soldiers have always been a credit to their country, on the beaches of Normandy as well as in the Loire valley, in the swamps of Korea or in windy Sweden. Our armed forces have never failed to do their job, and every Canadian worthy of the name can be proud of that.
The value of Canadians has been the object of many testimonials. Our soldiers have fought to safeguard freedom and democracy, which are part of the great values on which is based our way of life.
It should never be forgotten that there is no one without a beloved friend or relative
[Mr. Latulippe.l
buried in Europe. And those who did come back deserve a great deal of consideration. That is why I am particularly afraid that the changes brought about by the passing of the bill now before us will unjustly affect, in certain cases, the members of our armed forces.
With the modern equipment and the new tactics, it must truly be difficult for many of our soldiers to adjust themselves to the new military life. It is the duty of national defence officials to provide programs likely to enable our soldiers, if not to adapt themselves to new procedures, at least to adjust easily to civilian life and to the ever-changing conditions on the labour market in our country.
Mr. Speaker, there is a last point I should like to emphasize. I ask the Minister of National Defence to look closely into it, in order to take the necessary measures. I refer to the exodus of many of our young people, who after an intensive training as technicians or for some other trade in our armed forces, after the country incurred considerable expenses to enable them to have a career and learn a trade, emigrate to the United States to accept civilian jobs which are better paid than in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I ask the minister to render justice to our veterans and to take the necessary arrangements so that every Canadian who has been a member of the armed forces, where he spent part of his life, who has ruined his health to defend Canada, be treated properly, because he certainly deserves all the advantages to which he is entitled. In fact, there should be no shabbiness when our gallant soldiers who defended us so well are concerned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the remarks I will make will be very brief because I see no reason for repetition and many of the points I wish to stress have already been emphasized by previous speakers. Though I say I will be brief in order to avoid repetition, I also wish to point out that it is not because I concern myself with the fact that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) refers to anything over three minutes as a filibuster.
Quite often members have been inclined to say that because a debate may be prolonged in this house it is obstruction. This was the accusation made by one of the backbenchers on the government side just a week ago. However, I would like once again to stress the words of the Prime Minister who, on April 19, on a national television broadcast referred to the fact that so far as he was concerned the house had not done badly

in terms of work in the preceding 44 days leading up to that time. I firmly believe the house has been progressing somewhat better since then.
The white paper brought down by the minister has come in for a lot of comment. I notice he has been quite busy with the pencil when someone puts what he considers an important question. I only hope he will come up with some important answers because, as was stated by previous speakers, the white paper does not give information to the satisfaction of the house, but poses many questions that need answering. As previous speakers have said, what it contains has been pointed out on any number of occasions in the last few years. I am somewhat concerned about the attitude of the government and I have one very pointed question I wish to put to the minister, a question to which I think the house deserves an answer. I hope he will consider it important enough to take out his pencil and make a note of it. Where is the minister getting his advice? From whom is he getting it?
Very thorough briefs were presented by the three services to the special committee. The minister attended the committee meetings on a number of occasions and no doubt he has studied these briefs. But there were many questions left unanswered. I think particularly of the thoroughness of the brief presented by Admiral Rayner of the navy and the concern of the navy with regard to its future role in the defence of this country. Yet only about half a page is devoted by the minister to the navy in the white paper.
The minister has tried to leave the impression, which has caught on in most places, that tremendous savings have been achieved. In fact, on the same telecast of April 19 to which I referred the Prime Minister implied that if anybody studied the white paper he would see the economies that had been brought about. I should like to refer for a moment to what the white paper actually does say. If the Prime Minister or anybody on the government side of the house can show me where Canadian taxpayers are going to be saved any money by this move then I should like to know where it is. The white paper states:
The total savings to be effected as a result of such reductions will make available funds for capital equipment purchases, and eventually make possible more equitable distribution of the defence dollar between equipment and housekeeping costs. Sufficient savings should accrue from unification to permit a goal of 25 per cent of the budget to be devoted to capital equipment being realized in the years ahead.
As previous speakers have indicated, this is a matter of taking money out of one pocket
National Defence Act
and putting it in another, and there is no merit in the statement of the Prime Minister on the television broadcast of April 19 that integration is going to bring about economy. There has been much said about integration and since answers have not been forthcoming I assume that the minister looks upon integration as simply a matter of putting everybody in the same uniform. Up to now this is about the only clearcut explanation we have had. Everybody will be wearing the same uniform. But there has been no explanation whatsoever as to the method by which integration is going to be brought about.
Speaking of integration, I would point out that the question of the necessity for two ministers with defence portfolios has been brought up. Previous speakers have indicated that they have no wish to see the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) replaced by the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cardin) or vice-versa. However, I will be a little more specific and a little more blunt. I have heard it said by servicemen and by some Liberal backbenchers and others, and I firmly go along with it, that the background of the Associate Minister of National Defence qualifies him to take over as minister, that this would do away with the necessity of two portfolios in the defence department and that integration should start at that level. When the question of unification and integration was brought before the committee-Mr. Speaker, I would respectfully ask you to remind the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Teillet) that you have recognized me and that I have the floor. If he has something to say on the subject of national defence I am sure everybody on this side of the house would appreciate hearing him speak when his turn comes. In the meantime, since I have been recognized, I ask the hon. member to abide by the procedure followed in the house and to rise and make his remarks when the time allotted to me has expired.
Once again I emphasize that it has been said in certain quarters that the background of the Associate Minister of National Defence qualifies him far better for the position of minister than the hasty boy who now holds that office. When I say "hasty" I am not reflecting in any way on his ability to drive a motorcycle, but I do point out that the minister has been very hasty on other occasions. When he was in opposition he saw fit to rush things. He rushed them to the point where we could read his views in the newspapers before he had actually uttered them.
He seems to be following the same trend in the integration of the forces. His policy is rush, rush, rush, with no plans and no answers for the questions that will develop

National Defence Act
in such an undertaking. Integration has taken place in the upper echelons of the government. We only have to look at the Department of Agriculture to see it is being done. We also see it is not working out very well there, so possibly the minister should take a second look at what is going on there and then make a thorough study of integration and unification of the services before he rushes headlong into this matter.
The minister who today professes to be saving Canadian taxpayers $100 million is the same gentleman who only a few short years ago wanted millions of dollars spent on the Avro Arrow for the sake of establishing a Canadian air speed record. Of course, when he spoke in those days he spoke, as the original natives of the country used to say, with a forked tongue. Why do I say that? I entered into no obligation not to bring up this matter and the minister will recall the occasion. This same minister is fully aware of the fact that the government of which he was a member decided that the Avro Arrow was to be cancelled. This was a decision taken by the St. Laurent government of which he was a member, and this evidence was brought out by General Charles Foulkes.

speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, that allegation is not true. It is without any foundation whatsoever. I deny it categorically. The subject was never considered by the government before the election of 1957.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the rules provide that I have to accept the minister's word. But this only proves something else. When the general was testifying before the defence committee and made that statement the minister failed to tell him at that time that it was a lie. It is all right to get up in the house on a question of privilege and say this is not so and that it never took place. Why did the minister not get up and tell General Foulkes, who I understand was once reaching for a Liberal nomination, that his statement that the government of Mr. St. Laurent had decided to cancel the Avro Arrow but to postpone it because of the election was not true? Why did the minister not deny it at that time? Instead he gets up in the House of Commons on a question of privilege and denies what I have said, but he did not take the opportunity to deny it when the general was before the committee. He also never took the opportunity to deny the press reports of the general's statement, but he rises here on a question of privilege and says it is not so. I said before, Mr. Speaker, that the rules dictate I have to accept his word but I do so only because of the rules.
I have referred to the haste of the minister in announcing his integration policy. I have

referred to the submissions made by the representatives of the three services when they were before the defence committee. I point out to the minister that when the representatives of the services were questioned on the matter of integration, they were all of one opinion. It is recognized by all hon. members that one of the touchiest operations the government has in the defence department is to satisfy the demands made by the three services. This was quite clearly brought out in the committee. It was felt by all members of the upper echelon who appeared before the defence committee that possibly the unification of the services would stop this competition that goes on amongst the three services. They said, and at the time I believe everyone agreed or at least there was no denial of it, that this would be the effect.
However, what does the white paper say on this matter of eliminating competition amongst the services? I believe the word "jealousy" was used at that time. I refer to page 19 of the white paper, the third paragraph, where I read:
The sailors will press for more ships, the soldiers for more tanks and the airmen for more planes. This is as natural as breathing. Competition will not be lost but it will be contained at the service level.
The fact remains that the understanding we received was that unification of the services would eliminate competition. In the white paper the minister now claims that competition will be contained at the service level. Nevertheless, the sailors will press for more ships, the airmen for more planes and the soldiers for more tanks. The understanding given to us was that the reason the services would go along with partial integration was that it would eliminate this competition. This causes us to ask once again, where is the minister getting his advice? Who is advising him? I am quite sure from what has been said previously that the service chiefs have not had their way. Here again we get back to the basic fact that competition has been contained possibly at the service level.
I should like to say one more word on the matter of the approach of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer). As was stated by the previous speaker for this party, reference has been made to the nuclear role Canada has played and the reason this government undertook it. Reference was made also to the fact the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) considered it stupid; but the Minister of National Defence has taken so many different positions that no matter what is said in this argument he can say he said the same thing earlier. I would ask him to bear in mind that his own party has been breaking

promises. Although we had a newspaper advertisement here outlining the party's promises to a community, the Prime Minister denied them and the result has been that the community involved has just gone down the drain. The promise meant nothing.
The Liberals were going to renegotiate out of the nuclear role. I am not saying for one moment that the Canadian forces should not have the latest and best equipment available.
I do say the Liberals led the people of Canada to believe they were going to honour the commitments made by the previous government, and then renegotiate out of the nuclear role. Here we have the Bomarc sites in Canada armed with nuclear warheads, and they were not armed with nuclear warheads two weeks before the United States cancelled two of the six bases. There were supposed to be 32 bases constructed, but six were built. The moment Canada armed herself with nuclear warheads, the United States announced that two of these bases would be cancelled. I do not care whether the minister says it is the Bomarc A or the Bomarc B, the fact is the United States considered they were good enough to put into operation; but the moment Canada armed herself with nuclear warheads the United States cancelled two of these bases. In other words, we are filling in for them.
I feel it is about time this government finally realized there are a few election promises that they should carry out. As I have said, the minister has raced headlong into many problems. We have seen examples of this before. If the minister wishes to deny a statement made by General Foulkes, I would invite him to do what the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) did, that is impose himself on the C.B.C. and tell the nation that General Foulkes lied before the committee. In essence, this is what the minister is saying when he denies what General Foulkes said. He may as well go out and tell the nation that the man lied. I probably should go a little deeper into this question, but when I consider this is the Minister of National Defence who, on occasion, has asked us to forget what he has said about national defence, I ask the minister how he can expect this nation to reply upon anything he has to say.
