subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Hellyer for the second reading of Bill No. C-90, to amend the National Defence Act.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is the house ready for the question? I must caution the house that if the minister speaks at this time he will close the debate.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The Associate Minister of National Defence has already dealt with some of the questions raised by hon. gentlemen opposite. Tonight I should like to take this opportunity to deal briefly with a number of other questions which have been raised and elaborate on them a little.
Both the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) were critical of the fact that I limited my opening remarks to the terms of the bill now before the house rather than give a general review of defence matters. While in no way limiting the range of debate as far as hon. members are concerned, I considered that since a detailed statement on defence policy was contained in the white paper tabled less than two months ago, sufficient background was available and that any comments from me would have been repetitious in the circumstances.
The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) raised some general objections to the white paper. He said it was too generalized, that it lacked detail and that the first few pages contained little that is new. Well, the first part is a historical review. It was put in deliberately to give some of the background leading up to the changes in policy which we now propose for the decade that lies ahead. The balance of the paper is devoted to a general statement of policy-a general outline of the structure proposed by the government for the coming decade. Allegations have been made that white papers in the past have contained too much detail

National Defence Act
and too little about general policy-that too much space was devoted to lists of equipment and statistics and not enough to the outlining of future policy. I thought there was some validity in those allegations and for that reason in preparing a policy document we decided that the most important content of the present white paper must be the portion devoted to policy, and that once the policy had been laid down the staff work could go forward on the basis of that policy. The statistics relating to hardware and so on could be produced-as soon as the detailed staff work has gone forward on the basis of the general requirements as laid down in the white paper. This seems to me to be a proper and logical way in which to proceed-first, the general policy and then the details based on that policy.
The hon. member for Calgary North referred to the sheet which accompanied the publication of the white paper listing highlights, including the fact that there were a number of Glassco commission recommendations to be implemented. He asked what those recommendations were. Apart from the integration of the forces and increased responsibilities for the deputy minister as outlined in the white paper, many of these additional recommendations are in fact now being implemented, including the re-organization of the information services of the armed forces for the purpose of cutting down the total number of people involved and thus promoting economy, the preparation of estimates on the basis of programs of activity rather than on the basis of standard objects of expenditure, and so on. This, too, was mentioned in the section of the white paper which the hon. member found some difficulty in interpreting. I cannot at this time list in detail the various actions being taken by the department with regard to finance, personnel management, purchasing and supply, but I can assure the hon. member that the progress we have made is considerable.
The hon. gentleman said that two of the words used in the white paper, "flexibility" and "mobility", are old words which have been used on many occasions before. I agree they have been used on both sides of the house. What we need to do now is to get on with the action to provide the mobility and the flexibility to allow our forces to cope quickly and adequately with any situation which may require their attention anywhere in the world.
The hon. member seemed confused between the unification of the high command and the integration of the armed services. The white paper makes the point crystal clear on page 19. It says this:

...the integration of the armed forces of Canada under a single chief of defence staff and a single defence staff.. .will be the first step toward a single unified defence force for Canada.
I think it follows logically that once the high command has been unified and once the armed forces of Canada are organized on a functional basis rather than along traditional service lines the complete integration of the armed services will follow as a natural evolution from this change in organization. There will, of course, always be soldiers, sailors and airmen. We may also, some day in the future, have spacemen. But the duplication between two or more of the traditional forces is increasing and the overlapping is increasing; there are at the present time dozens of similar trades required by two or more of the armed forces of Canada, and there will be savings, and there will be economies and there will be a better use of manpower, once the forces have been organized on a functional basis, more particularly as integration proceeds.
The hon. member said an artillery officer could not command a destroyer. That may be so, but I suspect that an artillery officer might find himself quite at home with a naval gun after a brief familiarization period. Certainly many of the basic skills involved are the same. I think there should be no doubt left in anyone's mind as to what is intended: This unification of the command of the three armed forces is, as stated in the white paper, intended to be the first step toward a single unified defence force for Canada.
The question of civil control has been raised. Two or three hon. gentlemen have referred to the article by Brigadier Malone. I can assure the house that there is no problem in this respect. There will in fact be much better civil control in the future than has been possible in the past. The single defence staff will present its findings to the minister through the defence council, and before they are considered by the defence council they will be analysed fully by the appropriate section of the deputy minister's staff; that is, all proposals involving policy or the expenditure of public funds will be analysed by the civilian staff before they are considered by the defence council and before decisions are taken in respect of them. In addition, by using the defence council as-if I may use this term-a cabinet of the Department of National Defence, it will be possible to get a complete and full expression of opinion from both the senior civil advisers and the senior military advisers, so that all of the best opinion, advice and information available will be discussed and considered before decisions are taken. This will

permit, I believe, a more thorough examination of policy and of projects than has been possible in the past. It will permit a stronger civil control than has been the case, and it will also permit a better civilian direction in the sense that it will be possible to implement more closely defence policy as laid down by the government.
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) as usual made a very interesting contribution to the debate, and I appreciate his remark that his party will support Bill No. C-90. His main subject, however, was related to NATO strategy and his opposition to tactical nuclear weapons being employed in Europe. He suggested-and he can correct me if I am wrong-that more reliance should be placed on strategic nuclear weapons. There I disagree, since I consider that too much reliance on strategic nuclear weapons poses a far greater threat to peace.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, could I ask the minister a question? The minister has suggested that I should correct him if he is wrong. I should like to correct him right now, if I am in order in so doing.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: I stand corrected, Mr. Speaker, because I remember what the hon. member said. He suggested that reliance, for example, should be placed on Polaris seaborne missiles as an alternative to tactical nuclear weapons on the central front in Europe. Is that not correct?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the minister is now asking me a question. What I suggested was that the strike reconnaissance role could be more effectively carried out by Polaris weapons on submarines which were not vulnerable, rather than by strike reconnaissance aircraft, as at the present time.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is exactly what I
thought the hon. gentleman had said.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: It is the same type of weapon.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: It is with that, Mr. Speaker, that I would like to take issue, because first of all there is a difference in scale between seaborne or submarine Polaris missiles, for example, which are clearly in the strategic category, and tactical weapons such as those carried by tactical aircraft in the strike role.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, would the minister permit one other question? Does he not agree that the distinction between strategic and tactical weapons lies in the target, and if the target is a military one it can be properly defined as a tactical weapon; if, on the other hand, the target is behind the lines,
National Defence Act
as it were, civilians, cities, industries, and so on, then it becomes a strategic weapon at that stage?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I agree that this is a distinction.
I think the hon. gentleman should know, however, that the difference in degree of accuracy between seaborne and submarine-borne missiles such as he suggests, and those which would be carried by strike aircraft, makes all the difference in this case between strategic weapons and tactical weapons. Whereas a tactical strike aircraft can deliver with almost unbelievable precision its bomb or lethal load, whatever it is, to a military target, you could not possibly take that sort of a chance with a shipborne or submarine-borne Polaris missile, where the degree of accuracy is not adequate to permit its being used against a military target that happened to be, for example, in proximity to some urban or built-up area. There is quite a real and sharp distinction between these two systems. It is for this reason that I think considerable reliance must be put on tactical weapons as against strategic weapons, because strategic weapons are a weapons system of last resort. They are, in fact, directly related to the doctrine of massive retaliation which the hon. gentleman rejects.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The choices, if one relies solely on strategic weapons, are surrender or annihilation, and surely this is not what the hon. member really wants. The advantage of having tactical nuclear weapons is to provide a deterrence at a lower threshold than strategic retaliation. The NATO alliance does not have sufficient strength to deter aggression on the central front without tactical nuclear weapons. If our object is to deter war, we must face the reality of the situation. A greater reliance on strategic weapons would be the most dangerous and most provocative strategy that we could in fact employ.
In so far as Canada's contribution is concerned, we have already indicated in the white paper that the strike role will be reduced substantially in the years ahead. We have also decided to give our aircraft a second, non-nuclear capability. This gives the squadrons a greater flexibility under a wider variety of circumstances. This is directly in line with the policy set out a year ago. The hon. gentleman has mentioned several times what he refers to as intervention forces. In my opinion that is exactly what we are building up. Our forces are to be highly trained, mobile and flexible intervention forces, and I cannot really draw any distinction between the intervention forces that the hon. member suggests and those that are proposed in the

National Defence Act
white paper on defence. X think it is a question of semantics. If there is a distinction, I would like to know what it is, because I am not familiar with any distinction which might be in the mind of the hon. gentleman. He does not suggest that we should withdraw all our troops from Europe. What does he suggest as an alternative that we should do with those of our forces in Europe which are there for training, or other purposes, as part of our intervention forces? If he can suggest anything more practical and useful than what they are doing now, I think he has a responsibility to do so.
The question was raised on the other side of the house this afternoon as to the distinction between strike and reconnaissance roles. I may say that it was the previous government which put the strike and reconnaissance roles together as a single entity. In the white paper we tried to clear up this anomaly and be more precise by defining them as strike roles and reconnaissance roles, because in fact they are different and should be divided. The CF-104's which we have in Europe are now to be employed both in the strike and in the reconnaissance roles.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: And bombing.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The strike role, as we have often said, is a bombing role; there has been no question about that. I think this distinction should have been made long ago so as to avoid some of the confusion which has arisen in the minds of some people.
In respect to the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), may I say that what we have proposed at the present time is really a change which is designed to solve what was in fact for us a problem. It had previously been the plan to have some reconnaissance aircraft in each squadron. Under the new arrangement we are concentrating the six squadrons in the strike role in Germany and concentrating all of the aircraft which are engaged in the reconnaissance role in the two squadrons in France. In addition, as I have already said, all of these eight squadrons will have a second non-nuclear attack role. This is not a perfect solution but it is the best one we could devise in the present circumstances.
I appreciate the remarks of the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson), who in general supported the purpose of Bill No. C-90 and stressed the need for a strong, modern and completely mobile and efficient force.
The hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Lan-glois) gave his qualified support for the bill, but perhaps I might correct one part of his statement. He referred to the main headquarters being in Colorado Springs, and that the 
naming of a chief of the main headquarters would not alter the fact that this headquarters was outside Canada. Actually the headquarters at Colorado Springs is the joint command for North American air defence. The headquarters of the Canadian armed forces is, of course, in Ottawa. It is true that the deputy commander at NORAD is a Canadian. It is also correct that after many years of distinguished service Air Marshal Slemon is retiring shortly from this position, to be replaced by another distinguished Canadian, Air Marshal Dunlap, the present chief of the air staff.
The hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Langlois) also made certain allegations with regard to television repairs being carried out by service personnel of R.C.A.F. station, Uplands, in Ottawa. I do not in any way underestimate the seriousness of his charges, but I am sure that he will understand that if such charges are to be investigated more specific details will be required. I should therefore like to ask him if he would communicate with my office and furnish specific details to support his allegations. I can assure him that if he does so a thorough investigation will be made.
The hon. member for Hastings South (Mr. Temple) referred to remarks made by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) as to the percentage of the defence budget allocated to capital expenditures. The hon. member for Greenwood quoted from the report of the special committee to the effect that in the year 1963-64, 23 per cent of the budget was for new equipment. However, as the hon. member for Hastings South pointed out, this figure of 23 per cent did not relate solely to capital expenditures. The committee rightly said that 77 per cent of the total budget for 1963-64 is allocated for operations and maintenance, but the balance of 23 per cent includes not only equipment, but construction, NATO infrastructure and industrial applied research as set forth in the tables printed in the committee's report. The correct figure for equipment is approximately 13 per cent for this year, and it is this figure that we are out to correct in reducing headquarters strength and the consequent operation and maintenance costs.
The hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard) made reference to expenditures by NATO countries on defence, and in particular referred to the average of 8 per cent of the national budget of NATO members devoted to this purpose. He then went on to say that this compared to 25 per cent of the national budget spent by Canada. I think the hon. gentleman is confusing two things here, since in the former case it relates to the percentage

of the gross national product, while in the latter, in so far as Canada is concerned, the figure of 25 per cent is with regard to the annual financial budget at the federal level. To relate Canada's contribution to the 8 per cent of the gross national product of NATO countries, the figure given to the committee on defence for Canada was 5.1 per cent, placing Canada a shade below the middle of the scale among NATO nations.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. MacRae) made reference to two questions which he had on the order paper concerning what are known as "Nudets". These are nuclear detection and reporting stations. His question asked whether there were any of these units presently being constructed in Canada, and the answer given on the order paper was in the negative. He then referred to an article in the Saturday Evening Post of December, 1963 by Stewart Alsop, in which it was stated that a Nudets system was being built at 52 sites in the United States and southern Canada. May I say that in view of the wording of the question by the hon. member we had no alternative but to give the answer as stated, since in fact no such units were presently being constructed in Canada. However, I should like to assist the hon. member in any way I can in this regard.
First of all, this Nudets system referred to by Mr. Alsop does not relate to Canada. What has been done here is that in June, 1960 the government approved the construction of a number of nuclear detonation and reporting posts, known as N.R.P.'s around several target cities in Canada. A total of 25 such reporting posts were constructed under this program, with the Canadian army being the construction authority, at a total cost of $150,000. The United States Nudets system is designed for a similar purpose but is a far more sophisticated one than the Canadian reporting posts, and although there has been some suggestion that it would be advantageous to locate some United States Nudets in Canada, no such arrangement has been agreed to.
A number of general questions have been asked about our peace keeping operations in Cyprus. I know that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) will wish to make a statement following his return to Ottawa and I will leave discussion of this most important subject until then. One question which I should like to deal with, however, is this: Why was a French speaking unit sent to Cyprus? The reason is this. Le premier bataillon du royal vingt-deuxieme Regiment was for three years up to and including the time of the Cyprus crisis the stand-by battalion for UN requirements. In addition it was considered to be one of the
National Defence Act
best fighting units in the world. To deny this excellent unit its right to represent Canada would have been an injustice to the unit and to Canada.
One other question was raised with respect to peace keeping operations, and this was the suggestion that we do what some of the Scandinavian countries are now doing in putting together a special force for peace keeping operations. May I remind hon. gentlemen that at the present time all of the Canadian armed forces are on active service, and any part of the Canadian armed forces can be used for United Nations or other activities at any time. This does not require special legislation as is being proposed in one or two other countries.
We have forces available. We have used them on various occasions, and it is possible to use them on very short notice because they are trained and equipped for a wide variety of activities.

speechtext: May I ask the minister in this connection, why did he and his colleagues require a resolution of this house to send a force to Cyprus?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Actually, Mr. Speaker, a
resolution was required because of an undertaking on the part of the government to get such a resolution from parliament. It was a question of regard for the sovereign power of this House of Commons, something which my hon. friend raises from time to time.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: The minister knows it could have been done easier in two other ways.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard) raised the problem of the relationship of defence expenditures to industry, particularly in so far as they would be affected by disarmament. I can assure my hon. friend that there is no fear in this regard, and if he can achieve a multilateral arms control we will be happy to grapple with the economic consequences.
The most serious charge that has been laid is the suggestion that our defence capability has been steadily reduced. This suggestion is simply not true. One by one, our defence systems which were not operational are becoming operational. Our air defence system is far more effective than it was a year ago. As soon as the Genie rockets are available for our interceptor squadrons there will be another qualitative jump in effectiveness.
Six squadrons of our air division will soon become operational, and the two reconnaissance squadrons a few months later.
The acquisition of the M-113 armoured personnel carrier will dramatically increase the effectiveness and survivability of the

National Defence Act
Canadian army, and the brigade group in particular. This acquisition was long overdue. The first vehicles will be available later this year, and production in quantity will be available early next year. The acquisition of additional Caribou and Hercules aircraft increase substantially our flexibility and capability in air movements.
The navy's antisubmarine capability has never been higher, and the early paying off of some world war II ships in order to make additional funds available for new equipment is a forward move. There has been steady improvement in the capability of all arms and this improvement will continue in the months ahead.
No, Mr. Speaker, the white paper was not a publicity stunt. It is a broad policy chart for the next decade. It sets the foundation for the detailed planning and staff work which must go forward. It relates defence policy to foreign policy, and prescribes roles suited to the Canadian experience and personality. It predicts an organization which will permit the implementation of a coordinated, mobile and flexible force. It puts Canada in a position of leadership in military organization.
It is a good paper. This bill is a tool required to get on with the job. It is worthy of the support of this house.

There is one matter about which the parliamentary secretary might give us some information. Is there any information about the extent of the exemptions from sales tax that are granted to the provinces for the construction of hospitals, child caring institutions and one or two other similar types of institutions, if my memory serves me correctly, where refunds are made as a result of special circumstances? Is it the estimate of the Department of Finance that the two amounts will roughly balance? Is it expected that the amount to be paid by crown corporations under the federal government by way of provincial sales tax will more or less equal the amount now paid by the provinces under the federal sales tax levy?
This is a relatively simple measure. I know it will cure a lot of ill will that has existed. There was definitely a rub. I do not know

Crown Corporation Taxes whether the measure may lead to some sort of sales tax havens in this country. There are two provinces which do not have sales taxes at the present time and it may be that crown corporations will suddenly begin to do their business primarily in those two provinces. I do not know whether the provinces will then start, as some may suggest, to impose tariff barriers. Just what are we going to get out of this? There are still means whereby this measure can be circumvented, although it may be that the provinces will come to some agreement about sales tax equalization or there will be some method devised whereby purchases destined to another province will be subject to sales tax even though there is no sales tax within the province of destination. In any event, Mr. Chairman, we will be interested in seeing the bill and it is the conclusion of the official opposition that we will support this resolution.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PAYMENT OF PROVINCIAL TAXES AND FEES BY CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps it would be best if I were to deal with the questions raised by each speaker as we move along. We could perhaps facilitate consideration of the resolution in this manner. The hon. member for Edmonton West has raised the question whether or not the amount of sales tax crown corporations operated by the federal government will pay the provinces will balance with what is paid by the provincial agencies to the federal government.
I really do not think any figures are available in this regard. What we are doing in this resolution and in the bill which will be submitted to the house in due course is to achieve a balance as between the two senior levels of governments. Thus the present situation can continue whereby provincial departments are free of federal sales tax, and federal departments are free of provincial sales tax. On the other hand, the present situation where crown corporations and agencies of the provinces are bearing the federal sales tax but federal corporations are not paying the provincial sales tax will be changed. The result will be that crown corporations controlled by the federal government will be treated by the provinces in the same way as we treat corporations controlled by the provinces.
I do not think that the other question the hon. member raised with regard to tax havens is a very serious problem, because I really do not see this government or any federal government locating or carrying on the business of a crown corporation in a particular province in order to save the amount of sales tax that might be involved. I might at this point mention the fact that one can take the alternative view that all crown corporations,


whether operated by the provinces or the federal government, should be excluded from the sales tax.
I do not believe this is really a fair view to take, in that many of these crown corporations are actively competing with ordinary business organizations, and therefore I believe that crown corporations operating on this basis should have their financial result comparable to ordinary business concerns which are carrying on the same kind of business.

subtopic: PAYMENT OF PROVINCIAL TAXES AND FEES BY CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
The legislation which has been outlined by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance has been long overdue. There have been very strong feelings for years on the part of provincial governments that they have been required to pay federal sales taxes and many other federal imposts, whereas the federal government has not paid provincial sales taxes or gasoline taxes. What I think has been even more irritating has been the fact that the federal government has not even paid truck or car licence fees. Truck and car licence fees are not taxes in the ordinary sense, but they are a charge for using public thoroughfares. Heavy vehicles doing damage to the roads make no contribution either through gasoline taxes or through car and truck licence fees, and this has really caused a great deal of feeling. It is a matter which has been discussed at every federal-provincial conference that I recall since 1945, and probably was discussed long before that.
I am very glad that the government has decided to introduce legislation to make it possible for certain crown corporations to pay provincial sales taxes, gasoline taxes and car licence fees. When we have a look at the schedules, we will have a better opportunity to ascertain what crown corporations are affected and which ones have been exempted. I feel the day is coming when all government departments, as well as crown corporations, ought to pay taxes to both the federal and provincial governments. I believe this would be a much fairer thing for everyone concerned. I know many of the provincial governments feel strongly, for instance, about the fact that military equipment, which is extremely hard on highways when moving over provincial and municipal roads, makes no contribution whatever towards the maintenance of those roads. However this is another question which will be dealt with in due course.
At the present time the government is taking the first important step towards rectifying what is felt to be a very serious injustice in respect of federal-provincial relations. I am sure that most of the provincial governments will be delighted with the introduction of this legislation. They will feel

that they are now going to get some revenue to which they are entitled for the services which they give. This will place them on an equal basis with the federal government.
The other point which I feel has to be recognized is that, with the passage of time, there is more intervention by governments in the economy of the country. In spite of all the talk about pure free enterprise, the fact is that every government in Canada, federal and provincial, is doing a great deal more about public ownership than was done 30 years ago. I think this trend will tend to increase rather than diminish. If governments are going to go into business of any kind, either on a federal-provincial basis or on a shared basis with private corporations, then those crown corporations and government business enterprises should pay the same taxes as are paid by private companies to put them on a fair and equitable basis. I think the fact the federal government is going to pay these taxes now will place them on all fours with private companies, and will make crown corporations much more welcome to provincial governments than they have been in the past, when provincial governments felt they were going to supply all the services and were not going to get any of the revenue to which they were entitled. I congratulate the parliamentary secretary upon the introduction of this legislation on behalf of the government, and the members of this party will support it.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the present resolution precedes a bill the purpose of which is to appoint an additional puisne judge to the exchequer court. The object of this bill is also to amend the Judges Act so as to authorize the provision of salary for this additional judge.
It will be remembered that during the last session the house passed a piece of legislation which appears as chapter 10 of the 1963 Statutes of Canada, the short title of which is as follows:
Dissolution and Annulment of Marriages Act.
It will also be remembered that the purpose of this act is to authorize the Senate to dissolve a marriage by means of a simple resolution, in the cases where parliament dissolved marriages in the past. This legislation also makes it possible for parliament to review the resolution which provides for the dissolution of a marriage.
The bill which will follow this resolution seeks simply the authorization to confer on an additional judge of the exchequer court the powers of the divorce commissioner, an officer of the Senate whose appointment is provided for in chapter 10, as I said a moment ago, and who holds office at the present time.
In other words-and that was the objective of the house in passing chapter 10-it is important, as long as that matter of divorce remains in the hands of the legislative body- in this case, the Senate-that it be disposed of in the most objective, the most judicious and, I would say, the most "judicial" way possible.
It is important also, Mr. Chairman, that the man entrusted with this exacting mission, full of responsibilities, should see his prestige recognized by having the status of a judge of a superior court.
What the proposed legislation wants to do is to enable the Speaker of the Senate to appoint one of the judges of the exchequer

Judges Act
court to perform, in the future, all the commissioner's functions as provided for under chapter 10 of the statutes of 1963.
I also want to point out to the house that this legislation will not change in any way the effect and scope of chapter 10 I have just mentioned and will not give the exchequer court jurisdiction in divorce matters; this jurisdiction will remain solely in the hands of the Senate and the functions of the judge of the exchequer court who will have thus been appointed by the Speaker of the Senate will just have to hear witnesses, get evidence and report to the Senate in exactly the same way as the present commissioner.
Mr. Chairman, I think it should be noted that, besides the prestige given to the function and the guarantee that legal experience will be brought to the examination of the evidence, there will be the additional advantage that, in case of death, inability to act or illness on the part of the commissioner, it will be quite easy to replace him. All the Speaker of the Senate will have to do will be to designate, among the other judges of the exchequer court, one who will take over the duties of the commissioner.
I respectfully submit once again that this legislation will in no way change what the house decided during the last session, that it adds prestige to the function and that it facilitates, in case of illness or some other impediment, the temporary or permanent replacement of the official who will thereby be responsible for hearing the evidence and for reporting to the Senate.

Mr. Chairman, we are again happy to be able to support this bill, and we do so for several reasons. In my study of the field I would think that the former speaker had little to worry about because the constitution is clear on this matter of marriage and divorce. In the constitution it is stated that the federal government shall be responsible for marriage and divorce, and solely responsible. When a provincial government becomes involved with these matters it must pass legislation which endorses the legislation of the federal government.
It seems to me that the Senate was very unfair a year ago in refusing to pass a similar resolution, to be followed by a bill, to make the commissioner an exchequer court judge. I say this because of the fact that the Senate has had, or had at the time, the opportunity to examine the functions of this particular official and how they should be conducted. They have, of course, now had more time and are probably in a better position to assess the situation and allay any fears which they had. The Senate reports will indicate that by April 20 there had been introduced 218 resolutions, and to my knowledge none of them was rejected in any particular, or certainly on any major point. The Senate divorce committee have felt that none of the resolutions had been handled in a way in which they would not have been happy to handle them, had the law remained as it was in the past.
I believe that this present resolution is absolutely necessary, and for several reasons. First of all, we have asked the commissioner, who is a man of great legal knowledge, of good reputation and diligence, to accept an office which is a new one, and which would be objected to, it was felt in many quarters. He has accepted this office at the cost of his law practice. Therefore I believe he should receive the assurances and the pension which go with the office of an exchequer court judge because of the duty which he is performing, as well as in view of the fact that under present circumstances he might find himself without a job, should there be a change of government. This might not come about and we hope it does not; but in the past other officials who were commissioners and appointed by one government were not always maintained in their office by the succeeding government. In this case it would mean a severe loss, and I do not think we should ask anybody to assume this responsibility on this basis.

I should like to go a little further than the minister went, because it is my hope that when exchequer court sees fit to allow one of its members to act as a commissioner of divorce under the control of parliament and outside of the normal legal jurisdiction exercised by the exchequer court this would allow for a rotation system. I say that because I can see nothing worse than sentencing a man of the intelligence of the present commissioner to 15 or 20 years of hearing divorce cases four days a week at the rate of eight a day. This seems to me to be a sentence we should impose on no individual. I should like to see us arrive at a system which would allow for a rotation in the Senate, or at least a spelling off of the duties involved from time to time. It may be that as time goes by his duties may not require such an arduous schedule and that the exchequer court will be the beneficiary of this commissioner, and he will be able to handle other matters. It would also mean that in case of death of the commissioner it would be very easy to replace him with another commissioner under the same type of arrangement at the request of parliament.
Therefore, for these reasons I believe the house should give favourable consideration to this resolution. I hope the government has conferred with some of their confreres in the other place and that this bill will get speedy passage there as well. I am happy to note that because the former leader of the other place could not pass a similar measure we now have a new leader, and I hope the situation has improved. I believe this is a forward step. I have watched the operations of the commissioner. It is a new field. I have discussed on a number of occasions some of the problems which he has and I find that these problems are not much different from those we faced ourselves. I think this is an opportunity for parliament, and should be an opportunity for parliament, to examine the operations of that office periodically, at which time we should be prepared to make further recommendations in the whole field of matrimony and divorce.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the resolution stage I gave a rather full explanation of the resolution which is enacted in this particular bill. There are five main parts to the resolution and to the changes that we are proposing in this bill.
The first of these is that the estate tax will now be reduced by 75 per cent in provinces that levy their own succession duty, as was agreed at the federal-provincial conference here in Ottawa last year, provided they do not choose to take a payment equivalent to the additional 25 per cent instead. The second main point with respect to this bill is an amendment whereby the limit of $1,500 of funds which are available to beneficiaries from any one bank account is increased to $2,500. The third is a proposal that certain settlements under the Quebec civil code be treated similar to settlements of the same kind in the other provinces of Canada. The resolution stated this fact and it is enacted in the legislation.
The fourth point was that dispositions of community property in the province of Quebec be treated in the same way as they are treated by the succession duty act in the province of Quebec. The final item was to close a loophole with respect to a single premium annuity coupled with a life insurance policy whereby certain individuals, taking advantage of the provisions of the Estate Tax Act as it existed, were evading estate tax.

Mr. Chairman, there are a couple of omissions in the statement by the parliamentary secretary. If we look further into the bill we see there is also a clause dealing with penalties about which we have not heard anything. I should like to have an explanation of that clause. I am referring to clause 4 on page 5 of the bill. If the parliamentary secretary will consult his adviser I think he will be able to come up with the reasons why this change is being introduced.
I should like a full explanation because my experience with taxing statutes is that we have to be extremely careful about the
Estate Tax Act
penalty sections. Too often because of a sort of administrative zeal we get rather wide, sweeping provisions concerning penalties. Even as a result of innocent omissions or quite inadvertent errors in returns by taxpayers it is proposed that, notwithstanding bona fides on their part, they shall be subject to penalties for filing the wrong type of return. I must say I object to this. I think that very definitely there should be penalties where there is intent to deceive or conceal, but where the action by the taxpayer has been inadvertent I say it is wrong to impose additional penalties for failure to include certain things in returns. In my view this applies not only to the Estate Tax Act but to other taxing statutes which come under the jurisdiction of the Department of National Revenue.
I should also like to get some explanation, for the record in any event, with regard to why the amendment contained in clause 2 was included. I realize it must have come about as the result of some hard case where a really bona fide gift to charity was made with a right of encroachment and yet it was not possible to get renunciation in time before the death of the person who had the right of encroachment. I am not going to say too much about this provision included in the act. I have objected in the past that I thought that within certain limits there should be a right of encroachment on some of these gifts to charities, and that they should still be deemed to be gifts to charities perhaps to the extent that the encroachment was limited to a certain sum or a certain percentage of the charity.
I do not think it is quite fair to leave a widow for instance, to make a gift to a charity at a certain specified time, because she may be in necessitous circumstances or there may be a dependant child who will become subject to some misfortune and might have the right to encroach, and once that is cleared away that the gift be turned over to the charity and therefore become exempt from the estate tax.
Otherwise we have had a rather full explanation at the resolution stage. I presume that only time and experience will tell whether the language of these amendments will carry out the intent. I know that lawyers can engage in some very fine hair splitting on these matters and I certainly do not wish to comment on the language. I think it is reasonably straightforward, or as straightforward as language can be in a taxing statute. But I should like to have explanations as to the penalties and other matters.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if I may deal with the questions raised by the hon. member

Estate Tax Act
for Edmonton West, first of all I say thank goodness I am not a lawyer and therefore I cannot enter into legal arguments with him with respect to the wording, and whether or not it will carry out the intention as stated in the resolution which was discussed at some length. Clause 4 on page 5 was not included in the resolution and, as mentioned by the hon. member for Edmonton West, it is a penalty clause. It is a clause which is similar to section 56(2) of the Income Tax Act and it is designed to prevent gross negligence in the filing of returns with respect to estate tax. Perhaps I should read the wording of the clause into the record. It reads as follows:
Every person who, knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence in the carrying out of any duty or obligation imposed by or under this act, has made, or has participated in, assented to or acquiesced in the making of, a statement or omission in a return, statement or answer filed or made as required by or under this act or a regulation, as a result of which the tax that would have been payable if the tax had been assessed on the basis of the information provided in the return, statement or answer is less than the tax payable, is liable to a penalty of 25 per cent of the amount by which the tax that would so have been payable is less than the tax payable.
The intention of this clause is not to penalize the person who has innocently made a mistake or omitted something in filing a return. Anyone who prepares an estate tax return can inadvertently omit something. But just as section 56(2) of the Income Tax Act is designed to penalize those people who knowingly try to avoid paying the tax legally due to the Receiver General of Canada, so this section is inserted in the Estate Tax Act to provide similar penalties so as to prevent people from committing what really is fraud with respect to their taxes.
The other question raised had to do with clause 2 of the bill, and here I might perhaps quote an example. Let us take the example where a charitable gift is made by the husband with power to the widow to encroach and the widow does not renounce this gift within two years but dies within the two years without renouncing the right. The law will nevertheless allow a deduction in respect of the gift to the charity made by the deceased husband. It is a relieving provision in the act, and it is a beneficial amendment to the beneficiaries of the particular estate.

I am glad the parliamentary secretary has referred to sections 56 and 54(2) of the Income Tax Act. I know at the time these changes were made some years ago I was particularly insistent myself that in the framing of those sections they be limited directly to fraudulent intent or gross negligence. The original intention had been to

include negligence, and of course we must never have that.

Clause agreed to.
Clauses 2 to 6 inclusive agreed to.
Title agreed to.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day I put a question to the Minister of Justice based on a few words I had heard in the morning before the afternoon sitting.
The question I directed to the minister was as follows:
Did the minister say yesterday in Montreal that the federal government has set up in the privy council office a secretariat which will look after federal provincial relations?
The minister answered:
Mr. Speaker, I do not usually interpret my speeches but for more security I shall be pleased to send a dopy thereof to the hon. member.
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I want to point out that I have not asked for an interpreta-

tion; I merely asked for an answer and I hope that the minister, this evening, will understand my feelings in those circumstances.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, I have read the speech of the minister in both official languages of this country.

And having asked the minister if he had declared in Montreal the day before I posed the question whether or not he said the government had established a secretariat for federal-provincial affairs under the direction of the Prime Minister in the privy council offices, I then looked at the minister's speech, and I quote from his speech in Montreal in which he said:
In this respect I deem it a source of great hopes that a federal-provincial affairs secretariat is now established-
And I underline the words "is now established"
__within the privy council office under the
jurisdiction and direction of the right hon. Prime Minister.
I asked the question because today, as always, federal provincial relations are of great importance. Having read the minister's speech I then made an inquiry in the privy council offices, and what did I find? I found that one official in that office is, today, responsible for federal-provincial relations. This official is already occupied as an assistant secretary to the cabinet; therefore he can only devote a small part of his time to important questions of federal-provincial relations.
Mr. Speaker, along with other hon. members in this house, when I think of a secretariat for federal-provincial affairs, I think of a more sophisticated type of secretariat, the type that we might find in the resources field; a fully staffed secretariat, not reporting to one member government but to the council of ministers. The minister says the federal government has established a secretariat for federal-provincial affairs. No wonder he did not want to answer my question. What do I find? I find there is one part time official under the right hon. Prime Minister's direction in the privy council offices. No wonder Mr. Rene Levesque in the province of Quebec is becoming disillusioned by the spirit of co-operative federalism displayed by the federal government, whose centralizers persist in talking about co-operative federalism but do not practice what they preach. Again I say, Mr. Speaker, that upon investigation after the minister's declaration in Montreal, I find there is only one part-time official working on federal-provincial affairs in the privy council

offices. The minister says the federal government has established a secretariat for federal-provincial affairs, and I have quoted from his speech.
Today federal-provincial relations in Canada are worse than they have ever been before in the history of our country. We must improve co-ordinating bodies. I have suggested time and time again the immediate establishment of a secretariat for federal-provincial affairs at the Prime Minister's and premiers' level. I am not arguing the case for provincial rights or more centralization; I am only underlining the need for consultation. The minister states that a secretariat has been established, but in fact one has not been established. When will this government learn its lesson? Its whole economic program has foundered on the rocks, because they talk of consultation and sophisticated consultative bodies but do absolutely nothing about it. No wonder people like Mr. Levesque think that co-operative federalism is just a myth that will not work. He must realize that here in the government the centralizers have surrounded the Prime Minister and they do not mean what they say about co-operative federalism. How else could the minister have said that a secretariat has been established when, again I repeat, only one part-time official is working on the problem. I say again, Mr. Speaker, that the government must put this problem-

INQUIRY AS TO EXPORT ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reason I rise this evening is owing to the incident yesterday with regard to a question asked on agriculture. I see the Minister of Agriculture is not in the chamber, being I suppose unavoidably absent, but I note that his parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Peel, is present and I will direct my remarks to him.
The question reads as follows, as reported at page 3117 of Hansard:
With regard to his change in policy whereby the Minister of Agriculture has withdrawn the 30 cent subsidy paid by the government to the producers of cheese milk, will it now become compulsory and statutory that the cheese factories pay the cheese milk producers the 30 cents per
3206	HOUSE OF
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion hundredweight, since the government now proposes to pay the cheese factories a subsidy of 3.6 cents per pound for first grade cheddar cheese?
When that announcement was made by the Minister of Agriculture on April 29 that was the first thought which came to my mind, representing the interests of the cheese milk producers in my area. This also applies to similar areas of production represented by members of this house. This is a matter about which the government should be alarmed. That is why I asked in my question why the government does not make this compulsory and statutory so as to ensure that the farmer will still receive the same amount of subsidy, and therefore the same price, for his 100 pounds of milk as he did under the former administration and under the measures followed thus far by this government.
I am asking this question for further reasons. First of all, a factory which produces the average grade, which runs from 75 to 85 per cent No. 1 cheddar cheese, will receive 3.6 cents for the first grade. This would enable the factories to pay the farmer-and mathematics must rule in this case-scarcely 25 cents a hundred bonus for his milk, because only a part of the milk purchased is producing No. 1 cheese.
If they continue to pay the farmer 30 cents the factory would then be losing money on this arrangement. Second, a factory retailing ungraded cheddar cheese-and we have them in this country, particularly in eastern Canada-is not helped to receive the 3.6 cents per pound from the government because its cheese is not graded, and so this factory cannot pay the farmer any bonus for his milk. Therefore the change of policy announced by the minister indicates to me that he is leaving the farmer high and dry.
The minister says to the cheese factory: "We will pay you 3.6 cents per pound for all the No. 1 cheese you can produce, and you pay the farmer whatever deal you can make with him." That is the interpretation which is being placed on the minister's announcement.
The cheese industry is as nearly competitive with all other facets of the dairy industry as it has ever been, and many of the other interests in this industry would like to see cheese cheaper. Many of these other interests in the dairy industry would like to see cheese selling at a lower price. There is this friction between these interests in the industry, and cheese should not be used as a barometer nor as a lever. Once the government abandons one good measure of assistance, the cheese-milk producer and the small cheese factory sink that much more into oblivion, and this cannot be allowed to happen.


If I have any more minutes left, Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak of the cheese subsidy which has been so successfully employed to build up our export business in the last couple of years. One thing we should remember in our export policy is that high production and high prices very seldom coincide. For the last four years, total exports of cheese have increased and prices have advanced four cents per pound. This is a most unusual condition in the marketing of any type of merchandise. Removal or reduction of the export subsidy could adversely affect this trend.
Also, in respect of a small section of our dairy industry-and I refer to the Ontario cheese producers association, this section of the dairy industry which is still farmer controlled-the Canadian cheese marketing board has done a good job in the exporting of cheese, and it is only because it has done a good job that their supports are endangered and may be reduced. On the other hand, if they had not done a good job it is possible a seven cents subsidy might be required at the present time to export surplus cheese.
Larger production of cheese has been forecast for Canada during 1964, and to throw this production on the English market at a higher cost would jeopardize the future of the export business. The export subsidy is only on that part of cheese production that is exported, but the subsidy on butter is for the total production. The export subsidy as it exists at present must be maintained.

speakeroldname: Mr. B. S. Beer (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Forestry; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO EXPORT ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my opinion that the hon. member introduced two questions, the first being as to why the government does not make it statutory that the assistance of 3.6 cents per pound on cheese now being paid be paid direct to the producer. I suppose I would be justified in saying it would be a matter of government policy as to whether or not it would become statutory and, if it were to become statutory, it would be announced in due course.
In defence of the policy that has been announced, which indicates we will pay 3.6 cents on No. 1 cheddar cheese, it must be understood that you get approximately nine pounds of cheese out of 100 pounds of milk. If you multiply 3.6 by 9 you find it comes to something like 32.4 cents per 100 pounds of milk. This was more than was paid last year, so in fact nothing was taken away from the farmers. The assistance to the milk producers has always been paid through the milk suppliers, and this assistance will be paid by the distributors in exactly the same way.
The hon. member has also raised a question with regard to export assistance on cheese. I

think I should make it clear that this was never intended to be a subsidy on the export of cheese, but rather government assistance for the export of cheese which would enable our exporters to compete on foreign markets from the point of view of price. I have a statement to present at this time.
Up until 1961 export assistance was not paid on cheddar cheese. Rather the board, when the price of cheese dropped to the support level, took physical possession of the cheese and then or later, depending upon market conditions, offered it for export or to the domestic market at what was considered to be the best price obtainable. The difference between the support level and the price at which the board offered it for export could be considered to be the measure of export as-

In 1961 the level of Canadian cheddar cheese prices in Great Britain was such that the Ontario cheese producers marketing board was having difficulty financing, with its own resources, the export of cheese. The agricultural stabilization board then owned fairly large quantities of cheese bought under the support program.
